fetched_contents.text: Photovoltaic power estimation and forecast models integrating physics and machine learning: A review on hybrid techniques 1. Introduction The emergence of energy communities, microgrids, and virtual power plants requires precise power generation models. These models play a crucial role in simulating various scenarios and enhancing power forecasting for integration with the grid. Solar photovoltaic (PV) forecasting has attracted researchers from different fields such as meteorology, data sciences, and engineering, focusing on accurately estimating solar irradiance and converting it to electricity. Despite significant advancements in PV forecasting aimed at increasing reliability, current practices are still far from standardization [1]. The conversion of irradiance to power modeling typically follows two primary approaches: the physical and the data-driven methods. The former relies on a so-called physical model chain (PMC), a sequence of physical or empirical models characterizing irradiance to PV power, the latter explores the relationship between the PV power and irradiance from historical data. Physical modeling requires no historical data on the PV system and is appropriate for any term forecast. However, it has limitations: first, these physics-based models require detailed parameters designed specifically for a particular PV plant (PVP) and location, therefore, they are usually used for modeling MW-level PV farms and are less applied to residential rooftop PV systems [2]. Also, regarding their complexity, they require more domain knowledge to operate than data-driven approaches [3], as they are based on mathematical equations that describe the PV conversion. The algorithms employed involve the solution of complex differential equations which can require a large amount of computer power and time to give accurate predictions. Although the physical phenomena involved in PV conversion is nowadays well understood and modeled in sufficient fidelity, even mature and well-studied models introduce errors [4]. These models do not account for malfunction of the system or local effects on the irradiance, such as intra-hour power fluctuations caused by cloud movements, partial shading, or snow cover, which could be an argument for data-driven methods [5]. However, physical models are important tools when extended horizons are needed, as they usually outperform data-driven models for long-range forecasts [6]. Nowadays data-driven techniques have received significant attention to model the PV power. The advantage of this modeling approach is that it offers an alternative to conventional physical modeling, requiring no knowledge of internal system parameters. Instead of complex mathematical routines or physical representations, these techniques can learn the key information patterns from the data. Regression methods are frequently employed in this context, especially specific computing techniques based on kernel, neural networks, and ensemble methods have been successfully employed for intrahour to days-ahead horizons of PV power forecast [7], [8]. Although these data-driven methods demonstrate relatively strong forecast performance, they neglect the underlying physical principles governing PV conversion. As a result, their use is restricted to scenarios similar to datasets, presenting limited generalization applicability, and accuracy at the turning point of weather changes [9]. Comparisons of the physical and data-driven approaches have shown that the best model depends on the application, sometimes pointing out that physical forecasting models are better [10], sometimes that machine learning (ML) outperforms PMCs [11], or even that it varies depending on the training data quality and length [3]. The fusion between physics-based and data-driven models, the so-called hybrid modeling, has the potential to achieve both their advantages and assess individual deficiencies in estimation and forecasting. Physical models are applied to irradiance — PV power conversion or to adjust weather variables. Then, data-driven methods are used to improve the prediction accuracy or PV power estimation based on physics information [12]. The data-driven approach allows the model to account for unmodeled uncertainties and nonlinearities not captured by purely physical models, while the guidance of scientific theory makes the model less dependent on the data [13]. Different hybrid techniques have been effectively introduced for PV power forecast. These models are capable of joining the forces of the native methods by mitigating weaknesses of the singles to produce an optimized forecast for a range of time periods [14]. Recent literature reviews have extensively cataloged various methods for PV power modeling, with a predominant focus on more recent techniques based on ML and deep learning forecasting methods as in [7], [15], [16], [17]. In other reviews such as [18], [19], that present physical, data-driven, and hybrid models, the main focus on the individual methodologies makes the hybrid models receive scant attention. Despite the hybrid models limited coverage in published reviews compared with the individual approaches, authors in [15], [18], [20] point out their potential to increase the accuracy of individual models for PV power forecast, and in [6], [21], [22], [23] highlight the benefits of these models. Also, these reviews differ in terms of hybrid model definition. The hybrid models are sometimes defined as a “combination of physical and statistical/ML methods” [24]. In other works, they are defined as a “combination of two or more forecasting models,” including ensemble ML models [7], [15]. Furthermore, in terms of terminology used to refer to these models, they are called hybrid-physical, ensemble methods, knowledge-guided ML, and others. fetched_contents.text: Enhancing PV power forecasting through feature selection and artificial neural networks: a case study Introduction Solar energy is clean and abundantly available. Solar technologies utilize the sun to provide light, heat, electricity, etc. for domestic and industrial applications. With the alarming rate of depletion of major conventional energy resources such as coal, oil, and natural gas, coupled with the environmental degradation caused by the process of exploiting these energy sources, it has become urgent to invest in renewable energy resources that would sufficiently power us in the future without degrading the environment through greenhouse gas emissions. The solar energy potential is immense, but despite this unlimited solar energy resource, its harvesting is challenging, mainly due to the limited efficiency of photovoltaic cells. The demand for renewable electricity sources is rapidly increasing due to global efforts to reduce CO2 emissions1. Photovoltaic energy, in particular, plays a promising role for both developed and developing countries and is considered the most promising renewable energy source due to its advantages. Firstly, photovoltaic energy is clean, as it can produce electricity without emitting greenhouse gases and toxic gases such as CO2 and NOx. Additionally, it can have positive economic effects, not only because it reduces electricity bills after the initial investment, but also because the renewable energy sector has the potential to create new jobs. Furthermore, technologies harnessing solar energy are relatively easy to install on rooftops and can thus provide a means of producing clean electricity in rural areas. The potential for electricity production from photovoltaic converters essentially depends on the region where they are installed. Specifically, the production potential depends on average solar irradiation as shown in Fig. 12. The numbers indicated on the map presented in Fig. 1 show that solar energy provides a great production potential. However, the best conversion efficiency of most commercially available solar cells is in the range of 10–20%3. Although recent breakthroughs in solar cell technology show significant improvement, the fact that the maximum efficiency of solar cells still lies within the range of less than 20% indicates that there is a huge room for improvement. Algeria is indeed one of the largest solar energy deposits in the world with a duration of sunshine from 2000 to 3900 h per year, and a daily irradiation of 3000 to 6000 Wh/m2, equivalent to 10 times the global consumption which gives a great possibility of exploitation in this energy. The problems related to the integration of photovoltaic production into an electrical grid are becoming increasingly concerning, thus requiring the implementation of adequate solutions to mitigate the impact of these productions on the grid4. Among the main solutions envisaged are the development of forecasting and storage tools, thereby allowing the grid manager to anticipate and/or guarantee the level of production connected to the electrical grid. To address these challenges, the grid manager must anticipate variations in solar energy production and other intermittent sources over several time scales. This includes medium-term forecasting (j + 1, j + 2, j + 3), which allows for long-term energy supply planning and anticipation of demand fluctuations. In the short term (h + 1, h + 24), forecasting focuses on narrower intervals, facilitating real-time grid management and immediate decision-making to maintain the balance between supply and demand. Finally, in the very short term (m + 5), forecasting is done almost in real time, allowing for rapid response to sudden fluctuations in production or electricity consumption, including activation of available production means immediately. Thus, the development of forecasting and storage tools is essential to accompany these anticipations and ensure grid stability5. The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) techniques in the field of renewable energies is driven by the recognition of its potential. Many problems associated with renewable energies correspond precisely to the types of problems for which the AI approach seems most suitable. These computational models aim to simulate the cognitive and sensory functions of the human brain, exploiting this capacity to represent and manipulate knowledge in the form of models. Artificial neural networks (ANN), for example, use these models to model input–output functional relationships and can thus make predictions on other combinations of invisible inputs. AI techniques offer the potential for more accurate, faster, and more practical predictions than traditional methods6. Moreover, data from photovoltaic energy systems, being inherently noisy, are ideal candidates for processing by AI systems. Wan et al.7 presented an in-depth review of solar energy forecasting methods and their applications in the field of power grids. They classified these methods into four families of approaches, a statistical approach, an artificial intelligence (AI) approach, a physical approach, and a hybrid approach. Statistical approaches are based on statistical techniques in the field of time series analysis using historical data, such as the autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) method. AI approaches use the latest advances in the field of machine learning such as artificial neural networks (ANNs), decision tree forests (RF), support vector machines (SVM), etc. This category of methods can also be classified in the family of statistical approaches. Physical methods are part of the field of numerical weather prediction (NWP) using data from weather forecasts and satellite images. Hybrid approaches combine approaches from the three families of methods. fetched_contents.text: Metrics × Note: The Solar Forecast Arbiter is now under the stewardship of the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI). For more info, contact forecastarbiter@epri.com. The Solar Forecast Arbiter evaluation framework provides a suite of metrics for evaluating deterministic and probablistic solar forecasts. These metrics are used for different purposes, e.g., comparing the forecast and the measurement, comparing the performance of multiple forecasts, and evaluating an event forecast. Metrics for Deterministic Forecasts The following metrics provide measures of the performance of deterministic forecasts. Each metric is computed from a set of \(n\) forecasts \((F_1, F_2, \dots, F_n)\) and corresponding observations \((O_1, O_2, \dots, O_n)\). In the metrics below, we adopt the following nomenclature: * \(n :\) number of samples * \(F :\) forecasted value * \(O :\) observed (actual) value * \(\text{norm} :\) normalizing factor (with the same units as the forecasted and observed values) * \(\bar{F}, \, \bar{O} :\) the mean of the forecasted and observed values, respectively For more information on these metrics and others, see Zhang15, Wilks11 and the references listed below. Note that for normalized metrics (NMAE, NMBE, NRMSE), the Solar Forecast Arbiter currently allows no user control over normalization via the dashboard. Instead, the Arbiter has the following behavior depending on the forecasted variable type: * AC power: normalize using the AC capacity of the selected power plant * DC power: normalize using the DC capacity of the selected power plant * irradiance: no normalization; return normalized metric values as NaN * weather (e.g. wind speed): no normalization; return normalized metric values as NaN Additionally, the Solar Forecast Arbiter allows users to account for observation uncertainty by setting the error (forecast - observation) equal to zero for any point that is within a specified deadband, with the error unchanged for any point that lies outside the deadband. The deadband is specified as a percentage of the observation value at each time. A value of None indicates that no deadband was applied for that observation/forecast pair. Currently, the deadband is accounted for in the following metrics: MAE, MBE, RMSE, MAPE, NMAE, NMBE, NRMSE. The deadband is ignored for all other metrics. Mean Absolute Error (MAE) The absolute error is the absolute value of the difference between the forecasted and observed values. The MAE is defined as: \[\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \lvert F_i - O_i \rvert\] Mean Bias Error (MBE) The bias is the difference between the forecasted and observed values. The MBE is defined as: \[\text{MBE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (F_i - O_i)\] Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) The RMSE is the square root of the averaged of the squared differences between the forecasted and observed values, and is defined as: \[\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (F_i - O_i)^2 }\] RMSE is a frequently used measure for evaluating forecast accuracy. Since the errors are squared before being averaged, the RMSE gives higher weight to large errors. Forecast Skill (\(s\)) The forecast skill measures the performance of a forecast relative to a reference forecast (Marquez12). The Solar Forecast Arbiter uses the definition of forecast skill based on RMSE: \[s = 1 - \frac{\text{RMSE}_f}{\text{RMSE}_{\text{ref}}}\] where \(\text{RMSE}_f\) is the RMSE of the forecast of interest, and \(\text{RMSE}_{\text{ref}}\) is the RMSE of the reference forecast, e.g., persistence. Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) The absolute percentage error is the absolute value of the difference between the forecasted and observed values, \[\text{MAPE} = 100\% \cdot \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n | \frac{F_i - O_i}{O_i} |\] Normalized Mean Absolute Error (NMAE) The NMAE [%] is the normalized form of the MAE and is defined as: \[\text{NMAE} = \frac{100\%}{\text{norm}} \cdot \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \lvert F_i - O_i \rvert\] where norm is a constant upper bound on the value of the forecasted variable, e.g., the nameplate AC (DC) capacity of a PV plant when forecasting AC (DC) power. Normalized Mean Bias Error (NMBE) The NMBE [%] is the normalized form of the MBE and is defined as: \[\text{NMBE} = \frac{100\%}{\text{norm}} \cdot \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (F_i - O_i)\] where norm is a constant upper bound on the value of the forecasted variable, e.g., the nameplate AC (DC) capacity of a PV plant when forecasting AC (DC) power. Normalized Root Mean Square Error (NRMSE) The NRMSE [%] is the normalized form of the RMSE and is defined as: \[\text{NRMSE} = \frac{100\%}{\text{norm}} \cdot \sqrt{ \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (F_i - O_i)^2 }\] where norm is a constant upper bound on the value of the forecasted variable, e.g., the nameplate AC (DC) capacity of a PV plant when forecasting AC (DC) power. Centered (unbiased) Root Mean Square Error (CRMSE) The CRMSE describes the variation in errors around the mean and is defined as: \[\text{CRMSE} = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \left( (F_i - \bar{F}) - (O_i - \bar{O}) \right)^2 }\] The CRMSE is related to the RMSE and MBE through \(\text{RMSE}^2 = \text{CRMSE}^2 + \text{MBE}^2\), and can be decomposed into components related to the standard deviation and correlation coefficient: \[\text{CRMSE}^2 = \sigma_F^2 + \sigma_O^2 - 2 \sigma_F \sigma_O r\] where \(\sigma_F\) and \(\sigma_O\) are the standard deviations of the forecast and observation, respectively, and \(r\) is the correlation coefficient. ARMA is used independently in solar PV forecasting mainly for short-term, time-series problems where historical irradiance or power patterns are the dominant signal and where the data can be made stationary or otherwise compatible with ARMA assumptions. The evidence shows that ARMA is explicitly used to “develop forecasts” from historical solar power data and to “forecast hourly photovoltaic solar power generation,” suggesting it is especially suited to problems where the main forecasting task is to extrapolate a time series rather than to account for complex meteorological drivers or physical conversion mechanisms [N2-F1]. It is also used as a statistical method that can be embedded into more sophisticated decision-making models, indicating that it is well suited to settings where simplicity, ease of implementation, and parameter selection matter more than the need for full physical or machine-learning complexity [N2-F1].

For problems best suited to ARMA alone, the evidence points to hourly forecasting and short-term or deterministic forecasting. The ARMA-based solar power forecasting paper uses a year-long historical dataset and builds an ARMA(p,q) model for each hour, implying that ARMA is most effective when the time horizon is short enough that the time series can be localized and stationarity can be maintained per hour [N2-F1]. The same paper also notes that ARMA is used to forecast “hourly photovoltaic (PV) power generation,” reinforcing that it is appropriate for problems where the target is a regular, regularly spaced time series and where the forecast is not strongly constrained by exogenous weather inputs [N2-F1]. However, the evidence also warns that ARMA is limited by the need for stationarity and by the danger of overfitting when too many parameters are selected, so it is best suited to problems where the data are relatively regular and the stationarity can be enforced through preprocessing or by fitting only the best ARMA(p,q) model per time interval [N2-F1].

ARMA is fitted, validated, and tuned through a combination of statistical tests, model selection, and residual analysis. The solar power paper describes a step-by-step methodology that includes verifying stationarity for each time series, testing a number of ARMA(p,q) models, and using statistical tests on the residuals to validate the models [N2-F1]. It also mentions Bayesian information criteria (BIC) and choosing the best model, which is a standard model-selection approach for ARMA fitting [N2-F1]. The technical definition and core assumptions of ARMA further support this: ARMA models are built on stationary time series, with errors having mean zero, equal variance, and independence; the model assumes the time series distribution remains unchanged for arbitrary time shifts [N1-R2], [N1-R3], [N1-R4]. This means the model is fitted and validated under the assumption that the historical data already reflect the underlying stationary process, and that any exogenous variation must be handled separately or excluded. In the ARMA paper, the authors also note that the model is used to “build an ARMA model, to use statistical tests to validate it, and construct hourly samples,” which directly supports the claim that validation and tuning are done through statistical diagnostics rather than external performance metrics alone [N2-F1].

The limitations of using ARMA independently on solar PV data are significant. First, solar PV time series are not stationary in the classical sense: the paper explicitly acknowledges that ARMA has limitations [N2-F1], and the technical definition notes that ARIMA is used for non-stationary time series while ARMA is for stationary ones [N1-R1]. Solar irradiance and power output are inherently affected by weather, cloud cover, temperature, and other exogenous factors that can break stationarity and make pure ARMA less reliable [N4-F3]. The evidence also shows that feature selection and preprocessing are important for PV forecasting [N4-F3], suggesting that ARMA alone cannot easily capture the rich weather-related inputs that often drive PV output. Furthermore, the paper notes that ARMA is used “to generate samples for stochastic energy optimization models” and that it may inherit “nice properties for embedding into more sophisticated decision-making models,” but this also implies that it is less effective for capturing the nonlinearities and high-dimensional dependencies in real PV data [N2-F1]. Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that ARMA is best used independently for short, stationary, hourly PV forecasting, but it is limited when the data are non-stationary, highly exogenous, or nonlinear [N1-R1], [N2-F1], [N4-F3].

ARMA is commonly combined with other methods in hybrid solar PV forecasting through architectures that integrate ARMA with neural networks, SVMs, or other statistical/ML models. The evidence explicitly states that the most common approaches to improve solar irradiance forecasting are to combine ARIMA or other linear statistical methods with artificial neural networks, and that hybrid models are used to join the forces of native methods and mitigate weaknesses [N3-R3], [N3-F2]. The review paper also notes that hybrid models are sometimes defined as a “combination of physical and statistical/ML methods” and that they can combine two or more forecasting models, including ensemble ML models [N3-F2]. In the hybrid solar PV forecasting context, ARMA is often used as a statistical or linear component that can extract time-series patterns, while neural networks, SVMs, or other models are used to capture nonlinear relationships, temporal dependencies, or exogenous effects that ARMA alone cannot easily model [N3-F2].

Common hybrid architectures include ARMA + ANN, ARMA + SVM, and more generally hybrid-physical or knowledge-guided ML models. The evidence specifically mentions a novel hybrid model that combines ARMA with a nonlinear auto model for solar radiation prediction [N3-R2], and another hybrid model that combines ARIMA with artificial neural networks for improving irradiance forecasting [N3-R3]. The review paper also states that hybrid models can be used to combine physical and data-driven approaches, with physical models applied to irradiance–PV power conversion or weather variables and data-driven methods used to improve prediction accuracy based on physics information [N3-F2]. In practice, this means ARMA may serve as a feature extractor, a baseline predictor, or a preprocessing stage in hybrid models, rather than as the sole output generator [N3-F2]. The review further notes that hybrid models are used to produce an optimized forecast for a range of time periods and that they are especially useful when individual models have weaknesses [N3-F2]. Thus, ARMA is often integrated into hybrid systems not as the final predictor but as part of a multi-model ensemble or as a complementary component that stabilizes the system [N3-F2].

ARMA improves or complements other components in hybrid systems by providing a structured statistical baseline, capturing linear temporal dependencies, and often improving the overall robustness of the system. The evidence indicates that ARMA can be used to “generate samples for stochastic energy optimization models” and that it is easy to embed into more sophisticated decision-making models [N2-F1]. In hybrid systems, this means ARMA can help define the distributional properties of the forecast, provide a stable baseline, or generate synthetic data for downstream optimization and planning [N2-F1]. The review paper also states that data-driven methods can account for unmodeled uncertainties and nonlinearities not captured by purely physical models, while physical models provide guidance that makes the model less dependent on the data [N3-F2]. ARMA, as a linear statistical method, therefore complements these components by capturing the regular, linear part of the time series while other models handle the more complex or nonlinear aspects [N3-F2]. In solar PV forecasting, this combination is especially useful because the output depends on both historical irradiance/power patterns and weather-related exogenous inputs [N4-F3].

Trade-offs and implementation challenges in ARMA-based hybrids include increased complexity, computational burden, and the need to reconcile different model assumptions. The evidence shows that hybrid models are often designed to “join the forces of the native methods by mitigating weaknesses of the singles,” but this also implies that the resulting system can become more difficult to interpret, tune, and validate [N3-F2]. The ARMA paper notes that choosing a large number of parameters can inflate the likelihood and overfit the model, so model selection and tuning remain important [N2-F1]. The hybrid approach also requires careful handling of exogenous variables, preprocessing, and feature selection, which are common in PV forecasting [N4-F3]. Furthermore, the review paper warns that comparisons of physical and data-driven approaches show that the best model depends on the application, and that hybrid models are not uniformly superior across all settings [N3-F2]. Therefore, while ARMA-based hybrids can improve accuracy and robustness, they are not a panacea and require careful design, validation, and integration [N3-F2], [N4-F3].

Solar PV forecasting differs from general time series forecasting in three main ways: it is more strongly influenced by weather and exogenous inputs, it often requires shorter and more frequent forecasts, and it is usually embedded in a broader energy-management context. The evidence shows that solar PV forecasting is often driven by meteorological conditions and that PV generation is highly variable because it depends on meteorological conditions [N6-R2]. It is also described as being used for short-term and ultra-short-term forecasting, which implies that the horizon is much shorter than long-term forecasting and that the temporal structure is more tightly coupled to real-time or near-real-time decision-making [N6-R4], [N6-R5]. In contrast, general time series forecasting may focus on longer horizons, less frequent observations, or simpler stationary patterns [N1-R4]. The evidence also emphasizes that forecasting methods for solar power are broadly divided into physics-based, statistical, AI, and hybrid approaches, which further shows that solar PV forecasting is often treated as a specialized problem requiring both physical and data-driven methods [N4-F3].

Weather data, exogenous inputs, and temporal patterns all play essential roles in solar PV forecasting. The evidence repeatedly highlights meteorological variables and weather-related inputs as central to forecasting. For example, one review notes that solar irradiance forecasting is used to optimize energy systems and that weather data are important for prediction accuracy [N4-R3]. Another paper states that solar irradiance forecasting plays a key role in optimizing energy systems and that the literature summarizes techniques for predicting the effect of solar irradiance and temperature in solar PV applications [N4-R4]. The review paper also notes that data-driven approaches can learn the key information patterns from the data, but that they neglect underlying physical principles and may be limited in generalization and accuracy at the turning point of weather changes [N3-F2]. Exogenous inputs such as temperature, wind speed, and sky conditions are therefore not just ancillary; they are often the main drivers of forecast uncertainty and accuracy [N6-R4]. Temporal patterns are also important because solar PV output has a diurnal nature and can have large ramps, especially due to cloud cover and partial shading [N2-F1], [N4-F3]. This means that time series structure, seasonality, and temporal dynamics are not optional in solar PV forecasting; they are central to the problem [N4-F3].

ARMA is used or avoided in different forecasting settings depending on the stationarity, complexity, and exogeneity of the data. The evidence shows that ARMA is used when the time series can be made stationary and when the main forecasting task is to extrapolate historical patterns [N2-F1]. It is particularly suited to short, hourly forecasts where the time series can be localized and stationarity enforced per hour [N2-F1]. However, ARMA is avoided or limited when the data are non-stationary, highly exogenous, or nonlinear. The technical definition notes that ARIMA is used for non-stationary time series, while ARMA assumes stationarity [N1-R1]. The solar PV paper explicitly acknowledges that ARMA has limitations [N2-F1], and the review paper notes that data-driven methods can be restricted to scenarios similar to datasets and may have limited generalization applicability [N3-F2]. Therefore, ARMA is used in settings where the signal is relatively regular and the main challenge is forecasting the next time step, but it is avoided when the forecast depends heavily on weather, cloud dynamics, or exogenous inputs that break stationarity and introduce nonlinearity [N1-R1], [N2-F1], [N3-F2], [N4-F3].

Preprocessing and feature selection shape the input data for ARMA and hybrid models by reducing noise, capturing relevant patterns, and making the series more compatible with the assumptions of the forecasting method. The evidence shows that preprocessing and feature selection are important in PV forecasting, and that the best results are often achieved by systematically integrating feature selection techniques [N4-R2]. It also states that feature selection helps improve the accuracy and computational time of solar forecasting, though it is often passed by or conducted with limited rigor [N4-R5]. In the context of ARMA and hybrids, this means that preprocessing is not just about cleaning the data; it is about selecting the right features that can be modeled effectively by ARMA’s linear structure or by the hybrid components that may handle nonlinearities [N4-F3].

Common weather and temporal features used in solar PV forecasts include solar irradiance, temperature, wind speed, sky conditions, and other meteorological variables. The evidence explicitly mentions solar irradiance and ambient temperature as central variables [N4-F3], and another source notes that the literature summarizes techniques for predicting the effect of solar irradiance and temperature in solar PV applications [N4-R4]. Another source lists traditional meteorological variables such as temperature, wind speed, and ground-based sky data as inputs [N6-R4]. These features are important because solar PV output depends directly on irradiance and indirectly on temperature, cloud cover, and other weather conditions [N4-F3]. Temporal features are also important because the time series itself is the main input, and the paper notes that the solar irradiance forecasting paper uses a year-long historical dataset [N2-F1]. ## 1) How ARMA is used independently for solar PV forecasting

### Best-suited problems
ARMA is best suited to **short-term, time-series solar PV forecasting** problems where historical irradiance or power patterns are the dominant signal. The evidence shows that ARMA is used to “develop forecasts” from historical solar power data and to forecast “hourly photovoltaic solar power generation” [N2-F1]. It is also described as a statistical method that can be embedded into more sophisticated decision-making models, which implies it is especially attractive for settings where simplicity and ease of implementation matter more than full physical complexity [N2-F1].

The evidence further suggests that ARMA is well suited to **hourly forecasts** and to problems where the time series can be localized and stationarity can be maintained per hour. The solar PV forecasting paper builds an ARMA(p,q) model for each hour and uses a year-long historical dataset, indicating that ARMA is most effective when the forecasting task is regular and the time series can be treated as stationary at a fine temporal scale [N2-F1]. In contrast, the paper also explicitly acknowledges that ARMA has limitations, and the technical definition notes that ARIMA is used for non-stationary time series while ARMA assumes stationarity [N1-R1], [N1-R4]. This means ARMA is best suited to problems where stationarity is not too fragile and where the main signal is the past values of the time series rather than external weather drivers [N1-R1], [N1-R4].

### How ARMA is fitted, validated, and tuned
ARMA is fitted, validated, and tuned through a combination of **statistical tests, model selection, and residual analysis**. The solar PV paper describes a step-by-step methodology that includes verifying stationarity for each time series, testing a number of ARMA(p,q) models, and using statistical tests on the residuals to validate the models [N2-F1]. It also mentions Bayesian information criteria (BIC) and choosing the best model, which is a standard approach for ARMA fitting [N2-F1]. The technical definition reinforces that ARMA models are built on stationary time series, with errors having mean zero, equal variance, and independence, and that the model assumes the time series distribution remains unchanged for arbitrary time shifts [N1-R2], [N1-R3], [N1-R4]. This means the model is fitted and validated under the assumption that the historical data already reflect the underlying stationary process, and any exogenous variation must be handled separately or excluded.

### Limitations
The main limitations of using ARMA independently on solar PV data are that **solar PV time series are often non-stationary**, **highly exogenous**, and **nonlinear**. The evidence explicitly warns that ARMA is limited by the need for stationarity and by the danger of overfitting when too many parameters are selected [N2-F1]. Solar irradiance and power output are inherently affected by weather, cloud cover, temperature, and other exogenous factors, so pure ARMA cannot easily capture these drivers [N4-F3]. The paper also notes that ARMA is used “to generate samples for stochastic energy optimization models,” but that it may inherit “nice properties for embedding into more sophisticated decision-making models,” suggesting it is less effective for capturing the nonlinearities and high-dimensional dependencies in real PV data [N2-F1]. ## 2) How ARMA is combined with other methods in hybrid solar PV forecasting

### Common hybrid architectures
ARMA is commonly combined with other methods in hybrid solar PV forecasting through architectures that integrate ARMA with **neural networks, SVMs, or other statistical/ML models**. The trade-offs and implementation challenges in ARMA-based hybrids include increased complexity, computational burden, and the need to reconcile different model assumptions. The evidence shows that hybrid models are often designed to “join the forces of the native methods by mitigating weaknesses of the singles,” but this also implies that the resulting system can become more difficult to interpret, tune, and validate [N3-F2]. ## 4) Statistical preprocessing and feature selection that affect ARMA performance

### How preprocessing and feature selection shape input data
Preprocessing and feature selection shape the input data for ARMA and hybrid models by reducing noise, capturing relevant patterns, and making the series more compatible with the assumptions of the forecasting method. The evidence further suggests that ARMA is well suited to **hourly forecasts** and to problems where the time series can be localized and stationarity can be maintained per hour. The solar PV forecasting paper builds an ARMA(p,q) model for each hour and uses a year-long historical dataset, indicating that ARMA is most effective when the forecasting task is regular and the time series can be treated as stationary at a fine temporal scale [N2-F1]. In contrast, the paper also explicitly acknowledges that ARMA has limitations, and the technical definition notes that ARIMA is used for non-stationary time series while ARMA assumes stationarity [N1-R1], [N1-R4]. This means ARMA is best suited to problems where stationarity is not too fragile and where the main signal is the past values of the time series rather than external weather drivers [N1-R1], [N1-R4].

### How ARMA is fitted, validated, and tuned
ARMA is fitted, validated, and tuned through a combination of **statistical tests, model selection, and residual analysis**. The solar PV paper describes a step-by-step methodology that includes verifying stationarity for each time series, testing a number of ARMA(p,q) models, and using statistical tests on the residuals to validate the models [N2-F1]. It also mentions Bayesian information criteria (BIC) and choosing the best model, which is a standard approach for ARMA fitting [N2-F1]. The technical definition reinforces that ARMA models are built on stationary time series, with errors having mean zero, equal variance, and independence, and that the model assumes the time series distribution remains unchanged for arbitrary time shifts [N1-R2], [N1-R3], [N1-R4]. This means the model is fitted and validated under the assumption that the historical data already reflect the underlying stationary process, and any exogenous variation must be handled separately or excluded.

### Limitations
The main limitations of using ARMA independently on solar PV data are that **solar PV time series are often non-stationary**, **highly exogenous**, and **nonlinear**. The evidence explicitly warns that ARMA is limited by the need for stationarity and by the danger of overfitting when too many parameters are selected [N2-F1]. Solar irradiance and power output are inherently affected by weather, cloud cover, temperature, and other exogenous factors, so pure ARMA cannot easily capture these drivers [N4-F3]. The paper also notes that ARMA is used “to generate samples for stochastic energy optimization models,” but that it may inherit “nice properties for embedding into more sophisticated decision-making models,” suggesting it is less effective for capturing the nonlinearities and high-dimensional dependencies in real PV data [N2-F1]. Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that ARMA is best used independently for short, stationary, hourly PV forecasting, but it is limited when the data are non-stationary, highly exogenous, or nonlinear [N1-R1], [N2-F1], [N4-F3].

## 2) How ARMA is combined with other methods in hybrid solar PV forecasting

### Common hybrid architectures
ARMA is commonly combined with other methods in hybrid solar PV forecasting through architectures that integrate ARMA with **neural networks, SVMs, or other statistical/ML models**. The evidence explicitly states that the most common approaches to improve solar irradiance forecasting are to combine ARIMA or other linear statistical methods with artificial neural networks, and that hybrid models are used to join the forces of native methods and mitigate weaknesses [N3-R3], [N3-F2]. The review paper also notes that hybrid models are sometimes defined as a “combination of physical and statistical/ML methods” and that they can combine two or more forecasting models, including ensemble ML models [N3-F2]. In practice, ARMA is often used as a statistical or linear component that extracts time-series patterns, while neural networks, SVMs, or other models capture nonlinear relationships, temporal dependencies, or exogenous effects [N3-F2].

Common examples include ARMA + ANN, ARMA + SVM, and more generally hybrid-physical or knowledge-guided ML models. The evidence specifically mentions a novel hybrid model that combines ARMA with a nonlinear auto model for solar radiation prediction [N3-R2], and another hybrid model that combines ARIMA with artificial neural networks for improving irradiance forecasting [N3-R3]. The review paper also states that hybrid models can be used to combine physical and data-driven approaches, with physical models applied to irradiance–PV power conversion or weather variables and data-driven methods used to improve prediction accuracy based on physics information [N3-F2]. In practice, this means ARMA may serve as a feature extractor, a baseline predictor, or a preprocessing stage in hybrid models, rather than as the sole output generator [N3-F2].

### How ARMA improves or complements other components
ARMA improves or complements other components in hybrid systems by providing a structured statistical baseline, capturing linear temporal dependencies, and often improving the overall robustness of the system. The evidence indicates that ARMA can be used to “generate samples for stochastic energy optimization models” and that it is easy to embed into more sophisticated decision-making models [N2-F1]. In hybrid systems, this means ARMA can help define the distributional properties of the forecast, provide a stable baseline, or generate synthetic data for downstream optimization and planning [N2-F1]. The review paper also states that data-driven methods can account for unmodeled uncertainties and nonlinearities not captured by purely physical models, while physical models provide guidance that makes the model less dependent on the data [N3-F2]. ARMA, as a linear statistical method, therefore complements these components by capturing the regular, linear part of the time series while other models handle the more complex or nonlinear aspects [N3-F2]. In solar PV forecasting, this combination is especially useful because the output depends on both historical irradiance/power patterns and weather-related exogenous inputs [N4-F3].

### Trade-offs and implementation challenges
The trade-offs and implementation challenges in ARMA-based hybrids include increased complexity, computational burden, and the need to reconcile different model assumptions. The evidence shows that hybrid models are often designed to “join the forces of the native methods by mitigating weaknesses of the singles,” but this also implies that the resulting system can become more difficult to interpret, tune, and validate [N3-F2]. The ARMA paper notes that choosing a large number of parameters can inflate the likelihood and overfit the model, so model selection and tuning remain important [N2-F1]. The hybrid approach also requires careful handling of exogenous variables, preprocessing, and feature selection, which are common in PV forecasting [N4-F3]. Furthermore, the review paper warns that comparisons of physical and data-driven approaches show that the best model depends on the application, and that hybrid models are not uniformly superior across all settings [N3-F2]. Therefore, while ARMA-based hybrids can improve accuracy and robustness, they are not a panacea and require careful design, validation, and integration [N3-F2], [N4-F3].

## 3) Broader forecasting context and practical implications for solar PV

### How solar PV forecasting differs from general time series forecasting
Solar PV forecasting differs from general time series forecasting in three main ways: it is more strongly influenced by **weather and exogenous inputs**, it often requires **shorter and more frequent forecasts**, and it is usually embedded in a broader energy-management context. The evidence shows that solar PV forecasting is often driven by meteorological conditions and that PV generation is highly variable because it depends on meteorological conditions [N6-R2]. It is also described as being used for short-term and ultra-short-term forecasting, which implies that the horizon is much shorter than long-term forecasting and that the temporal structure is more tightly coupled to real-time or near-real-time decision-making [N6-R4], [N6-R5]. In contrast, general time series forecasting may focus on longer horizons, less frequent observations, or simpler stationary patterns [N1-R4]. The evidence also emphasizes that forecasting methods for solar power are broadly divided into physics-based, statistical, AI, and hybrid approaches, which further shows that solar PV forecasting is often treated as a specialized problem requiring both physical and data-driven methods [N4-F3].

### Roles of weather data, exogenous inputs, and temporal patterns
Weather data, exogenous inputs, and temporal patterns all play essential roles in solar PV forecasting. The evidence repeatedly highlights meteorological variables and weather-related inputs as central to forecasting. For example, one review notes that solar irradiance forecasting is used to optimize energy systems and that weather data are important for prediction accuracy [N4-R3]. Another paper states that solar irradiance forecasting plays a key role in optimizing energy systems and that the literature summarizes techniques for predicting the effect of solar irradiance and temperature in solar PV applications [N4-R4]. The review paper also notes that data-driven approaches can learn the key information patterns from the data, but that they neglect underlying physical principles and may be limited in generalization and accuracy at the turning point of weather changes [N3-F2]. Exogenous inputs such as temperature, wind speed, and sky conditions are therefore not just ancillary; they are often the main drivers of forecast uncertainty and accuracy [N6-R4]. Temporal patterns are also important because solar PV output has a diurnal nature and can have large ramps, especially due to cloud cover and partial shading [N2-F1], [N4-F3]. This means that time series structure, seasonality, and temporal dynamics are not optional in solar PV forecasting; they are central to the problem [N4-F3].

### Why ARMA is used or avoided in different forecasting settings
ARMA is used or avoided in different forecasting settings depending on the stationarity, complexity, and exogeneity of the data. The evidence shows that ARMA is used when the time series can be made stationary and when the main forecasting task is to extrapolate historical patterns [N2-F1]. It is particularly suited to short, hourly forecasts where the time series can be localized and stationarity enforced per hour [N2-F1]. However, ARMA is avoided or limited when the data are non-stationary, highly exogenous, or nonlinear. The technical definition notes that ARIMA is used for non-stationary time series, while ARMA assumes stationarity [N1-R1]. The solar PV paper explicitly acknowledges that ARMA has limitations [N2-F1], and the review paper notes that data-driven methods can be restricted to scenarios similar to datasets and may have limited generalization applicability [N3-F2]. Therefore, ARMA is used in settings where the signal is relatively regular and the main challenge is forecasting the next time step, but it is avoided when the forecast depends heavily on weather, cloud dynamics, or exogenous inputs that break stationarity and introduce nonlinearity [N1-R1], [N2-F1], [N3-F2], [N4-F3].

## 4) Statistical preprocessing and feature selection that affect ARMA performance

### How preprocessing and feature selection shape input data
Preprocessing and feature selection shape the input data for ARMA and hybrid models by reducing noise, capturing relevant patterns, and making the series more compatible with the assumptions of the forecasting method. The evidence shows that preprocessing and feature selection are important in PV forecasting, and that the best results are often achieved by systematically integrating feature selection techniques [N4-R2]. It also states that feature selection helps improve the accuracy and computational time of solar forecasting, though it is often passed by or conducted with limited rigor [N4-R5]. In the context of ARMA and hybrids, this means that preprocessing is not just about cleaning the data; it is about selecting the right features that can be modeled effectively by ARMA’s linear structure or by the hybrid components that may handle nonlinearities [N4-F3].

### Common weather and temporal features
Common weather and temporal features used in solar PV forecasts include **solar irradiance, temperature, wind speed, sky conditions, and other meteorological variables**. The evidence explicitly mentions solar irradiance and ambient temperature as central variables [N4-F3], and another source notes that the literature summarizes techniques for predicting the effect of solar irradiance and temperature in solar PV applications [N4-R4]. Another source lists traditional meteorological variables such as temperature, wind speed, and ground-based sky data as inputs [N6-R4]. These features are important because solar PV output depends directly on irradiance and indirectly on temperature, cloud cover, and other weather conditions [N4-F3]. Temporal features are also important because the time series itself is the main input, and the paper notes that the solar irradiance forecasting paper uses a year-long historical dataset [N2-F1]. In addition, the review paper emphasizes that data-driven methods learn the key information patterns from the data and that PV forecasting involves intrahour to days-ahead horizons [N3-F2]. This implies that time lags, seasonal patterns, and temporal structure are treated as features in the forecasting pipeline [N3-F2].

### How exogenous variables are integrated into ARMA-based models
Exogenous variables are integrated into ARMA-based models through preprocessing, feature selection, and hybrid architecture design. The evidence shows that solar irradiance forecasting is used to optimize energy systems, and that the literature summarizes techniques for predicting the effect of solar irradiance and temperature [N4-R4]. It also states that feature selection is used to enhance PV power forecasting [N4-R2]. In hybrid models, exogenous variables are often handled by including them as inputs to the data-driven component, while ARMA may be used to model the time-series component or to generate baseline forecasts [N3-F2]. The review paper further notes that hybrid models can combine physical and data-driven approaches, with physical models applied to irradiance–PV power conversion or weather variables and data-driven methods used to improve prediction accuracy based on physics information [N3-F2]. In practice, this means exogenous variables are integrated by preprocessing them into the model inputs, selecting the most relevant ones, and combining them with the time series structure before fitting ARMA or other components [N4-F3], [N3-F2]. The evidence therefore supports the conclusion that preprocessing and feature selection are central to ARMA performance in solar PV forecasting, and that they are especially important when the forecast depends on weather-related exogenous inputs rather than just historical patterns [N4-F3], [N4-R2], [N6-R4].

## Conclusion

Overall, the evidence supports a clear picture of how ARMA is used in solar PV forecasting: **independently as a simple, stationarity-driven time-series model** for short-term, hourly forecasts, and **in combination as a hybrid component** that augments neural networks, SVMs, or other models to capture nonlinearities and exogenous effects. The best-suited problems for ARMA alone are those where the time series is regular and stationarity can be enforced; the best-suited problems for ARMA in combination are those where the forecast depends on weather, cloud dynamics, or complex temporal patterns. Across all settings, preprocessing, feature selection, and careful handling of exogenous variables are essential, and the evidence shows that ARMA is often used because it is easy to implement and embed into decision-making models, but avoided when the data are non-stationary, highly exogenous, or nonlinear [N1-R1], [N2-F1], [N3-F2], [N4-F3].
